You are being evaluated on Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream of ARC-style grid puzzles.
Each puzzle instance has a task id and a test input grid. Tasks recur across the
stream with fresh inputs. Each instance is a separate conversation: the next one
starts without this one's messages.

On every message you must choose exactly one action and put it as a JSON object
on the last line of your reply:
  {"action": "submit", "grid": [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5]]}   submit an output grid
  {"action": "request_demos"}                            ask for one more demonstration pair for this task
  {"action": "finish"}                                   end the instance, once it is over
Grids are lists of rows; cells are integers 0-9; dimensions are 1-30.

Each demo request returns one more input-output pair of the task, up to the demo cap shown
with the input.

Scoring: an instance you solve costs 1 for each wrong submission and 1 for
each demo request. An instance is over when a submission is correct or when the attempt
cap is reached, and one that ends unsolved costs the whole budget, 16, however
many submissions and demo requests it used. Feedback on a submission is only
correct/incorrect. There is no way to abandon an instance, and finish is refused until
the instance is over. Each instance is scored on its own, and lower cost is better.

Color-6 rectangles r0-3,c7-8; r1-3,c10-12; r2-3,c17-18; r5-10,c7-11; r5-11,c13-17; r9-11,c1-3; r9-12,c19-20; r12-13,c9-11. Coordinates are zero-based inclusive. Correct all non-5/6 noise within the rectangles to the patch color, and all other speckles to background 8. Critical boundary check: the large 6 patch at c13-17 ends at r11; r12 c13-17 are background (one 1 speckle), even though r12 c19-20 are 6 and another 6 patch starts at c9-11. Initial wrong answers incorrectly extended c13-17 through r12. A second wrong hypothesis extended the r1-3,c10-12 6 patch upward to r0 based on 1 clue and background cells; this was incorrect. Verify exact row/column bounds instead of extrapolating.

Bounds zero-based inclusive. Fill non-background corruptions within each rectangle to its color (including 4/3 marks), and clear all outside speckles to background 9. Notable boundaries: r14-15,c15-21 is 2x7, including r14c21 corruption and r15c21 8; color-5 c15-16 patch ends at r12, separate from c4-5 patch; 8 rectangle at c19-23 ends r11."), ('arc_fill_diagonal_parity_bands', 'ARC: fill periodic bands from clue lines', "Continual-ARC task-d5aa1daf: tile the grid with periodic color bands indicated by the geometry of the clue lines. First determine orientation from the input: full horizontal clue rows imply a row-periodic, row-uniform output; diagonal clues aligned down-right imply colors depend on d=r-c. Do not assume every recurrence instance uses the same orientation. Infer the period and residue-to-color map from clue positions/colors; a useful first candidate is the smallest period for which no two clues in the same residue class disagree. Preserve clue colors and fill the whole grid.

Confirmed horizontal case (current 25x25): clue rows r=4:3, r=6:7, r=17:9, r=23:1. Minimum consistent period is 4, giving row colors by r mod 4: [3,9,7,1]. This solved the instance. A 13x13 demo had horizontal clues and period 7, row-color residues [9,2,1,4,8,5,9]; clue rows agreed with this pattern. Thus periods vary; don't infer period as unique-color-count or count+1.

Confirmed diagonal cases: a demo had periodic d=r-c bands with period 5 (one residue-to-color sequence across diagonals; output rows shift by one each row). Earlier solved 27x27 example had d=-16 and d=7 colored 1, d=-6 colored 5, consistent with period 3: color 5 when d mod 3=0, otherwise 1. Another confirmed instance had colors 5 at d=5 and 6 at d=10 and alternating parity bands. Infer period/palette from the actual clues rather than hard-coding a palette, period, or orientation.

Important zero-background case (confirmed on 2x2 task recurrence): zero cells are empty/background, not clue colors. A 2x2 input [[9,3],[0,9]] has nonzero clues on down-right diagonals d=r-c: color 9 at d=0 and color 3 at d=-1; the 0 at d=1 is not a conflicting clue. Minimum consistent period is 2, so fill all cells by d parity (even=9, odd=3), yielding [[9,3],[3,9]]. Do not treat zeros as clues when inferring residue maps; preserve/fill nonzero clue colors.

Additional confirmed recurrence (20x20): clue bands were anti-diagonals with constant s=r+c, not down-right d=r-c. Lines s=2 and s=28 were color 7; line s=33 was color 9. Correct output used period 3: s mod 3 = 0 -> 9, residues 1 and 2 -> 7. A period-2 parity fill (7 on even, 9 on odd) fit every clue but was submitted and marked incorrect. Therefore do not blindly use the smallest period consistent with clue colors: the clue-line geometry may support a larger period. This recurrence's three distinct clue-line positions map exactly onto the three period-3 residues. Determine orientation from constant coordinate (r-c for down-right lines; r+c for down-left/anti-diagonal lines), then infer period using the full geometric clue arrangement; validate that outputs shift correctly.

Related demos confirm outputs are full periodic bands, not merely clue preservation: a 5x5 diagonal example had d=r-c period 3 with residues [3,5,2] by d mod 3 = [0,1,2]; a 20x20 example had d=r-c period 6. Horizontal cases also use row periodicity. These are task-specific examples, not a fixed universal period.

Confirmed horizontal recurrence (30x30, task-d5aa1daf): clue rows r=0:9, r=1:7, r=8:2, r=27:2, r=29:8. Period 5 yields row colors by r mod 5 = [9,7,2,2,8], and filling every row uniformly with this cycle solved the instance. Five clues cover all five residues and are consistent.

Confirmed horizontal recurrence (17x17, task-d5aa1daf): nonzero clue rows r=1:4, r=3:1, r=4:4, r=6:8, r=8:5, r=11:5. Minimum consistent period is 6; the clues cover all residues, giving row colors by r mod 6 = [8,4,5,1,4,5]. Fill every row uniformly with this cycle; submission confirmed correct. This reinforces use of the minimum consistent period when clues cover each residue, while retaining caution for geometries where larger period is indicated.

Confirmed horizontal recurrence (9x9, task-d5aa1daf): zeros are background/empty; treat every nonzero row color (including 9) as a clue. Clues: r=0:5, r=2:2, r=3:1, r=4:9, r=5:9, r=6:9, r=8:9. Smallest consistent period is 7 (smaller periods collide on differently colored nonzero clues); the clue rows cover all seven residues, yielding row colors by r mod 7 = [5,9,2,1,9,9,9]. The correct output repeats this row-color cycle. Important: do not mistake a frequent nonzero color such as 9 for background; here 0 is background. A prior p=6 guess from treating the 9s as empty was wrong.

Additional horizontal demos reinforce this rule: a 21x21 instance with background 0 and clues r=0:4,r=7:6,r=9:2,r=14:7 had period 4 and residue colors [4,2,7,6]; an 11x11 instance with background 0 and clues r=1:6,r=3:8,r=4:8,r=6:9 had period 4 and residue colors [8,6,9,8]. In both, infer the smallest period consistent with nonzero clue rows, map colors using row indices modulo that period, and tile full uniform rows."), ('arc_compare_two_binary_panels_at_their_shared_color', 'ARC: compare two binary panels at their shared color', 'Continual-ARC task-638c72af (confirmed correct on multiple recurrences). A uniform separator row or column divides the grid into two equal-sized panels; omit it and compare cells at identical coordinates. Each panel is binary; let S be the single color shared by both panels. Output has one panel’s dimensions, is filled with color 3, and uses S at each coordinate where EITHER corresponding input cell is not S. Equivalently: output 3 only where BOTH corresponding cells equal S; otherwise output S. Do not reverse these output colors. Examples: demo with S=9 outputs 3 at common-background locations, 9 where either panel has a non-9 speckle. Confirmed test with upper colors {8,1}, lower {1,4}, separator row [0,0], S=1; compare top rows 0–13 to input rows 15–28. Correct output: [[1,1],[1,3],[1,3],[1,1],[1,3],[1,1],[1,1],[3,1],[1,1],[3,1],[1,1],[1,3],[1,3],[1,1]]. Careful: bottom panel starts immediately after separator (row 15 in this 0-indexed 29x2 case); map all 14 rows in order.

Additional confirmed recurrence (task-638c72af, test input 2x19): a zero separator column divides two 2x9 panels. Left panel uses {6,7}, right uses {4,6}, so the shared color is S=6. Compare identical coordinates: output is 3 only where both panel cells equal 6, otherwise 6. Row 0 had no coordinate where both were 6, yielding [6,6,6,6,6,6,6,6,6]; row 1 shared 6 only at column 3, yielding [6,6,6,3,6,6,6,6,6]. Submission was confirmed correct.

Additional confirmed recurrence (29x2): [8,8] separator row at index 14 splits 14x2 panels (top rows 0–13, bottom rows 15–28). Top colors {7,9}, bottom {5,7}, shared S=7. Apply rule rowwise: output 3 iff both aligned cells are 7, else 7. Confirmed correct output: [[7,3],[3,7],[3,7],[7,3],[3,7],[7,3],[7,3],[3,3],[3,7],[3,3],[7,3],[7,3],[3,7],[7,7]].


Additional confirmed recurrence (15x14): uniform separator row at index 7 splits two 7x14 panels; colors top {8,1}, bottom {7,1}, shared S=1. Output remains 7x14 and is 3 only at coordinates where both aligned cells are 1, otherwise 1. In this test there were no shared-1 coordinate overlaps, so the correct output was a uniform 7x14 grid of 1s. Be careful to compare equal relative panel rows: bottom row index is separator+1+relative_row (here input row 8+r), not an unrelated row. A first incorrect candidate marked row3/col1 due misaligning a bottom marker; exact coordinate comparison shows none.

Additional confirmed recurrence (17x29): a uniform zero separator column at index 14 splits 17x14 panels (left columns 0–13, right columns 15–28). Left colors {9,2}, right colors {5,9}, shared S=9. Correct output is 17x14, 3 only where aligned left and right cells are both 9, otherwise 9. The 0-based coordinates producing 3 were (0,2), (1,10), (2,2), (2,9), (3,0), (5,5), (6,3), (8,1), (8,13), (9,10), and (13,0); submission confirmed correct with no wrong attempts.

Additional confirmed recurrence (12x15): uniform separator column 8 at index 7 splits two 12x7 panels, left columns 0–6 and right columns 8–14. Left colors {1,2}, right {1,4}, shared S=1. Compare same row and relative column. Output dimensions 12x7; output is 3 iff both aligned cells are 1, else 1. In the test, right-side 1 speckles were at (r0,c3), (r3,c2), (r5,c5), (r10,c2), (r10,c4) using panel-relative c; left-side 2 markers invalidate overlap at (r3,c2), so correct 3 positions are (0,3), (5,5), (10,2), (10,4). First submission incorrectly included (3,2) by overlooking the left marker; corrected output confirmed. Practical caution: explicitly scan for left-panel nonshared-color markers at candidate overlaps.'), ('arc_color_the_trailing_gap_after_a_horizontal_marker_row', 'ARC: color the trailing gap after a horizontal marker row', 'Continual-ARC task-b4235fd4. Fill color is always 1; background and marker colors vary. Core rule: for each intended multirow marker-pattern group, identify its rightmost marker extent. Color the trailing background suffix to the right edge only on rows with a horizontal marker run reaching that group’s rightmost extent; preserve marker pixels and all other cells. Do NOT treat every isolated 8-connected island inside a dense patterned band as its own fill target: that causes large overfills. Likewise, a lone marker at the maximum column in a row is not enough if it does not form the horizontal marker run (confirmed current test: lower 4x22 pattern has max marker col20; rows21 and23 have horizontal 4-runs ending at c20, so only their c21 cells become 1; rows22 and24 have isolated c20 markers and remain unchanged. Upper band ends at c21, so has no trailing suffix). This exact output solved the current test on the third submission after (wrong) attempts that independently filled 8-connected islands and then filled c21 on all four lower rows.

Confirmed demos: (1) bg2/fg0, row0 run c0-2 and trailing suffix c3-8 -> 1; full marker rows with no trailing space unchanged. (2) bg0/fg6, upper group max c9 reached by row1 -> fill c10-14 only; lower group max c12 reached by row8 -> fill c13-14. (3) bg5/fg2, row0’s rightmost horizontal run c7-8 ends at c8 -> c9-10 become 1; the later group had marker at far edge and stayed unchanged. (4) bg0/fg2, top group has rightmost marker c17 in rows0-2 -> c18-19 become 1 in all three; lower group reaches edge c19 and stays unchanged. (5) bg4/fg9, upper group reaches edge c17 and stays unchanged; lower group has rightmost c12, rows15 and17 horizontal runs to c12 and fill c13-17. In that demo row16 also had c13,c15,c17 changed to 1 while even c14,c16 remained bg; preserve as observed, not fully explained by the simple rule. Another earlier demo with bg4/fg9 changed only row0 c28 (between a final 9 marker at c27 and 4 at c29); indicates avoid assuming all pattern objects have simple one-color backgrounds.

Past failure: my first attempt used 8-connected components and filled suffixes after each island, causing overfill. My second attempt colored c21 on all four rows of the lower band; only rows with a horizontal run to the group max were eligible. Prefer grouping the visually coherent multirow pattern and applying the rightmost-horizontal-run criterion; preserve all unrelated pixels.

(6) New confirmed test (task-b4235fd4; bg9/fg8; 29x11): top group rows0-2 has row0 singleton marker at c2 and rows1-2 markers c0-1; correct output colors row0 c3-10 with 1, leaving the other rows unchanged. Lower group rows12-14 has a full horizontal marker row c2-10 reaching the right edge, so no suffix is added. Thus a singleton can qualify when it is the leading/rightmost row of this multirow pattern group (do not apply the isolated-marker exclusion without considering its role in the group). Initial all-unchanged submission was wrong; one demo confirmed the fill color 1 and suffix rule. Demo examples showed groups like rows3-4 and 7-8 with horizontal runs reaching edge unchanged, while a final group row16 c2-3 was filled c4-8.'), ('arc_fill_gaps_between_aligned_markers', 'ARC: fill gaps between aligned markers', 'Continual-ARC task-0e26539b (confirmed by a correct submission): On a grid with background color and marker pixels (demo: background 1, markers 6; prior test: background 7, markers 8; another test: background 9, markers 0), keep every marker unchanged and fill background cells with color 3 when they lie strictly between two markers on the same row or column. Apply across each aligned marker interval; cells outside those intervals stay background. Checking adjacent markers in sorted row/column order is sufficient because the union of intervals between any pair equals the union of intervals between consecutive markers. Example: three markers in one column at rows 1, 2, and 5 cause rows 3-4 between the latter pair to become 3. Additional confirmed demo evidence: with background 4 and marker 9, all strictly-between cells on aligned rows/columns become 3 (not 9); e.g. row 0 markers at columns 10 and 13 fill columns 11-12 with 3, and row 2 markers at columns 1 and 12 fill columns 2-11 with 3. A lone marker (demo: background 6, marker 8) remains unchanged. In test background 2/marker 0, the gap likewise became 3; filling it with 0 was incorrect. Rule: fill only cells that were background and lie in a row/column interval bracketed by at least two markers; preserve marker pixels. Latest confirmed test (background 9, markers 1) also followed the same rule: row intervals included r3 c7–15, r8 c12–18; vertical markers in column 11 at rows 2, 5, and 7 filled intervening rows 3–4 and 6. A marker pair at r7 c10–11 is adjacent and adds no cells. The successful output confirms fill color 3 and the union-of-horizontal-and-vertical intervals.')]
